In 2023, the United Nations inBahrain embarked on the development of a new United NationsSustainable Development
Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) for 2025-2029 with the Government of Bahrain (GoB) to replace the outgoing
Strategic and Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (SCF) for 2021-2024. The new UNSDCF promotes
a coherent and coordinated strategy to implement the United Nations 2030Agenda for Sustainable Development while
contributing to the attainment of Bahrain’s Economic Vision 2030 and the Government Plan 2023-2026: I) Raising
the Living Standard of Citizens to Preserve their Gains, II) Justice, Security and Stability, III) Economic Recovery
and Sustainable Development and IV) High-quality and Competitive Government Services. It seeks to accelerate the
implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by capitalizing on key enablers. It was developed under
the principles of the United Nations Development System Reform, using the new guidelines for the next generation of
United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. Launched in 2019, the reform places development
at the heart of the United Nations, emphasizing the UN’s 2030 Agenda and the 17 SDGs. It aims to reposition the
United Nations as a stronger, better-defined collective identity and a trusted, reliable, cohesive, accountable, and
effective partner to countries working towards the 2030 Agenda.
These priorities are supported by four core outcomes, aiming towards universal access to quality services and
resilient public spaces, a diversified and inclusive economy bolstered by sustainable practices, governance structures
that guarantee justice and human rights, and robust environmental stewardship, driving sustainable and inclusive
development in harmony with global goals and national visions. Partnerships, which are central to the 2030 Agenda,
are mainstreamed across all four strategic priorities.
The United Nations Country Team (UNCT) in Bahrain led by the United Nations Resident Coordinator, is composed of
representatives of 22 United Nations agencies, funds and programmes UNAFPs working jointly to support the country
in achieving its development priorities aligned with the SDGs. Seven UNAFPs are physically present in Bahrain while
14 are Non-Resident Agencies (NRA).
In signing, the partners endorse this UNSDCF and emphasize their joint commitment towards fulfilling its objectives.
The UNSDCF will be reviewed yearly by a Joint Steering Committee (JSC) of the GoB and the UNCT, thereby allowing
the Government and the United Nations to reassess the designated areas of work and strengthen and adapt as
needed, with the goal of accelerating progress towards achieving the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and
Bahrain’s Economic Vision 2030.
Joint Statement
The priorities identified in the Cooperation Framework are:
Strategic Priority Area 1: People — Enhanced Social Equity and Well-Being
Strategic Priority Area 2: Prosperity — Sustainable Economic Transformation
Strategic Priority Area 3: Peace — Governance for Justice and Human Rights
Strategic Priority Area 4: Planet — Resilient Environmental Stewardship

Executive Summary
The UNSDCF for Bahrain (2025–2029) represents a strategic
partnership between the United Nations and the Kingdom of
Bahrain, designed to advance the country’s ambitious journey
towards sustainable development, equity, and prosperity.
Rooted in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
and closely aligned with Bahrain’s Economic Vision 2030
and the Government Plan 2023-2026, the UNSDCF focuses
on transformative actions that cater to the evolving needs
of Bahrain and its people. Through an inclusive consultative
process involving a broad range of stakeholders, including youth
groups, women, workers, trade unions and representatives for
people with vulnerabilities1, this framework outlines a unified
approach to tackle the multifaceted challenges of sustainable
development, while seizing opportunities to foster resilience,
inclusivity, and economic diversification.
The UNSDCF is tailored to Bahrain’s unique context and
characteristics as a small, open, high-income, post-oil economy
with a large body of expatriate workers, a highly climatevulnerable arid, island city state with key geostrategic position
in the Gulf. The UNSDCF is also cognizant of the last-mile
development challenges of the country where the Government
already has the fundamental structures and mechanisms
for service delivery and social protection in place. It aims to
accelerate SDG implementation by leveraging key enablers
like digitization, artificial intelligence, and financial inclusion,
while integrating youth into the development process.
Bahrain’s commitment to sustainable development is
underscored by its proactive measures to align national
priorities with the SDGs. The UNSDCF leverages this
alignment, focusing on four strategic priorities: enhanced social
equity and well-being, sustainable economic transformation,
governance for justice and human rights, and resilient
environmental stewardship. These priorities encapsulate a
holistic approach to development, integrating economic, social,
and environmental dimensions to ensure no one is left behind.
This alignment was achieved through a comprehensive
consultation process that included diverse representation from
Bahrain’s diverse societal segments, ensuring that the voices
of youth, women, workers, and populations with higher needs2
were integral to the planning and decision-making processes.
Innovations and strategic partnerships stand at the forefront
of the UNSDCF’s implementation strategy. Recognizing the
importance of collective action, the framework emphasizes
the United Nations’ role in bringing together Government,
civil society, private sector, and international partners to cocreate solutions that are sustainable, scalable, and impactful.
Key innovations include the integration of digital technologies
to enhance public services, the promotion of green
economy principles for environmental sustainability, and the
development of inclusive policies that ensure equitable access
to opportunities for all citizens, especially the most vulnerable3.
Adopting a system thinking perspective, the UNSDCF for
Bahrain recognizes the dynamic interplay between various
components of the national development ecosystem. Informed
by a comprehensive understanding of this interconnectedness,
the Framework is designed to be adaptive, responsive to
changes, and grounded in the complex reality of Bahrain’s
socio-economic landscape.
The theory of change underpinning the UNSDCF articulates
a clear pathway towards achieving sustainable development
in Bahrain. It acknowledges the interdependencies among
the strategic priorities and outlines the necessary conditions,
actions, and partnerships to facilitate transformative change.
By addressing key preconditions such as enhancing
stakeholder capacity, aligning laws with international human
rights standards, and promoting gender mainstreaming, the
framework sets a solid foundation for progress towards the
SDGs.
The United Nations’ comparative advantage in Bahrain lies
in its ability to provide integrated policy advice, technical
expertise, and global best practices. Through a tailored UNCT
configuration, the framework mobilizes the collective strengths
of resident and non-resident United Nations entities to deliver
cohesive and impactful support across all strategic priorities.
This collaborative approach ensures that the UN’s interventions
are complementary and synergistic, maximizing the potential
for sustainable development outcomes.
As Bahrain continues to navigate the complexities of the
21st century, the UNSDCF serves as a testament to the
country’s dedication to sustainable development and the
UN’s commitment to supporting these efforts. By fostering an
environment of innovation, inclusivity, and partnership, the
UNSDCF aims to accelerate progress towards a prosperous,
equitable, and sustainable future for all people living in Bahrain,
contributing to the global pursuit of the 2030 Agenda.
In this document, the term ”people with vulnerabilities or higher needs” refer to people that may face specific challenges in accessing opportunities and services, necessitating targeted support and resources to improve their wellbeing. In Bahrain, these groups are acknowledged as integral parts of the nation’s diverse social fabric. The final definition of people with vulnerabilities or higher needs will be jointly shaped through bilateral negotiations between
United Nations Agencies, Funds, and Programmes (UNAPFs) and relevant line ministries or technical departments, ensuring a context-specific and collaborative approach tailored to Bahrain’s unique landscape.

Chapter 01
The 2030 Agenda is a pledge to ensure social inclusion,
environmental protection, and economic development that is
both sustainable and inclusive, to do so in partnership and
peace. It is universal in scope and each of the 193 United
Nations Member States are developing their own path to
achieve this ambitious agenda.
The 2030 Agenda commits to ‘Leave No One Behind’ (LNOB)
and support the furthest behind first in a manner that targets
their specific challenges and vulnerabilities. This generates an
unprecedented demand for local and disaggregated data to
analyse outcomes and track progress. The 2030 Agenda rests
on the interconnected and indivisible nature of its 17 goals.
The 2030 Agenda embraces five critical dimensions: People,
Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership, also known as
Bahrain’s national development priorities are guided by
its Economic Vision 2030, focusing on sustainability,
competitiveness, and fairness. The vision aims for a diversified
economy less reliant on hydrocarbons, improved human
capital, efficient Government institutions, an enabling regulatory
framework, world-class infrastructure, and enhanced social
services. The Vision 2030’s implementation involves four-year
Government plans with specific pillars and objectives aligned
with the SDGs.
The 2019-2022 GoB Plan focused on striking a fiscal
balance between expenditure and revenue while continuing
its economic growth, diversification of sources of revenue,
monetary stability and comprehensive development. It aimed
to transition the public sector’s role from economic driver to
regulator, in partnership with the private sector, to support
innovation and improve citizens’ living standards.
The GoB has been making significant progress towards the
country’s Economic Vision 2030 – which largely harmonizes
with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Bahrain’s Voluntary National Reviews (VNR) in 2018 and
2023 highlighted achievements, challenges, and priorities
for SDG acceleration but also revealed the need for tangible
the ‘5Ps’. Traditionally viewed through the lens of three core
elements – social inclusion (People), environmental protection
(Planet), and economic growth (Prosperity) – sustainable
development has evolved into a richer concept with the
adoption of the 2030 Agenda, which builds upon this traditional
approach by adding two critical components: Peace and
Partnership.
At the heart of this Cooperation Framework between the United
Nations and the Kingdom of Bahrain, and of all contemporary
United Nations-supported development efforts, resides a wider,
ambitious, and holistic pursuit of the realization of a ‘better and
more sustainable future for all,’ without leaving anyone behind
and reaching the furthest behind first.
In 2021, the Government introduced the Economic Recovery
Plan, a five-pillar plan to stimulate economic recovery, mitigate
the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and update the Fiscal
Balance Plan. This plan supports labour market reform,
regulatory reform, strategic projects, and the development of
priority sectors to boost Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth
in the non-oil sector. The 2023-2026 Government Plan, «From
Recovery to Sustainable Growth,» shifts focus to sustainable
development across six policy pillars: sovereign and legislative;
infrastructure and environment; economic recovery and fiscal
sustainability; community services; improving standard of
living; and Government performance and digital transformation.
These pillars align with the 2030 Agenda’s five dimensions:
people, prosperity, planet, partnership, and peace.
commitments and funding to ensure progress. As outlined in
the 2023 VNR, Bahrain has seen an acceleration in addressing
environmental challenges, investment in renewable energy,
digitization, emergency and disaster preparedness, as well as
enhancing fiscal sustainability challenges.

In particular, towards the goal of enhancing social equity and
well-being, Bahrain has made significant strides in providing
universal access to healthcare and education, supported by
constitutional reforms and the establishment of the Ministry
of Sustainable Development (MoS) in June 2022 to ensure
alignment of Government policies and plans with the SDGs.
A key achievement was the management of the COVID-19
pandemic, emphasizing a whole-of-Government approach, and
adopting innovative health strategies for infection prevention
and control, as well as equitable access vaccines for all persons
living in Bahrain. The Government also provided a financial
and economic stimulus package amounting to BHD 4.5 billion,
to counter the economic impact of the pandemic. In 2022, the
country achieved its target set in 2013 to provide 40,000 new
housing services to citizens and launched innovative affordable
housing initiatives in partnership with the private sector.
Challenges identified around the 2030 Agenda include fiscal
sustainability for transformative investments and the need for
accurate, timely data for monitoring progress towards theSDGs.
Data gaps, particularly in climate action, sustainable cities,
gender equality, and peace, justice, and strong institutions,
hinder effective monitoring and implementation of the SDGs.
To address this challenge, the MoS has been coordinating the
collective efforts of Government agencies to make available
accurate, timely, relevant, and quality disaggregated data to
measure progress and strengthen evidence-based national
policies. Working closely with United Nations agencies, the
Ministry strives to increase awareness, provide technical
training and review the current data processes with the aim of
adopting global best practices.
The country has made consistent investments in improving the
digital infrastructure, use of technology, and financial inclusion
and as key enablers for SDG acceleration.
Bahrain has also demonstrated a strong commitment to
strengthening migration governance. In 2018, Bahrain
supported the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular
Migration (GCM). This commitment aligns with Bahrain’s
dedication to international cooperation in addressing migration
issues and implementing policies that are linked to the
GCM’s objectives. Bahrain’s support for the GCM signifies its
recognition of the importance of a comprehensive, cooperative
approach to managing migration and protecting the rights and
dignity of all.
Achievements around creating a sustainable economic
transformation include the Bahrain’s Economic Vision 2030
focus on sustainability, competitiveness, and fairness, aiming
to double household disposable income by 2030. Strategies for
economic diversification, including strategies for the Industrial
Sector, Tourism Sector, Logistics Services and Financial
Services Sector Development Strategies (2022-2026), helped
to increase significantly the non-oil sector contribution to
economic growth. Efforts to empower the private sector and
foster entrepreneurship have led to an estimated investment
of USD 12 million, and attracted a record level of foreign direct
investment (FDI) inflows with the country’s FDI stock reaching
USD 42 billion in 20234. The development of sustainable
tourism supporting investments in culture and communitycentered creative industries are aligning with sustainable
development solutions and international cultural conventions.
Bahrain has achieved a nation-wide 5G network coverage
and made significant progress in ensuring financial inclusion
of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), women and youth,
including through advancement of financial technologies
(Fintech) and Islamic products.
In the area of governance for justice and human rights,
Bahrain’s constitution promotes peace, tolerance, gender
equality, and access to justice for all citizens. Bahrain has
actively participated in regional and international forums
to shape the SDGs, showcasing its commitment to justice
and human rights. It was the first country in the Cooperation
Council for the Arab States of the Gulf (GCC) region to develop
a National Human Rights Action Plan (NHRAP), which was
approved in 2023. Bahrain retains the Tier 1 ranking in the
US Department of State’s report on Trafficking in Persons for
the seventh consecutive year.

progress made to advance gender equality for Bahraini
women in respect of education, employment opportunities, and
facilitating increased political participation of women.
Around environmental stewardship, Bahrain reduced a
fifth of its freshwater withdrawals and increased water-use
efficiency by 80 percent in line with the National Water Strategy
2030. It has adopted the National Adaptation Investment Plan
and launched the new National Energy Strategy committing
to doubling renewable energy targets by 2035 through largescale solar power projects and solar financing schemes.
Initiatives such as the First National Blacklist of Invasive
Species and comprehensive national food security strategies
have been formulated to protect the environment and promote
sustainability.
Gaps and Opportunities
The UNSDCF 2025-2029 has been designed to build on
the significant progress Bahrain has made, with a focus
on areas with potential for further improvement to achieve
the last mile, leveraging Bahrain’s unique characteristics,
challenges and strengths. As outlined in the VNR 2023, the
country has made significant strides in providing access to
healthcare, education and basic services to all its citizens.
It’s management of the COVID19 pandemic, which included
provision of widely accessible vaccines to all citizens and noncitizens in the country was a global good practice. To sustain
and build on the progress so far and to fully achieve the 2030
Agenda, efforts are needed to address remaining disparities

Bahrain's strategic location within the GCC together with
its high level of integration with the region presents unique
opportunities and challenges that significantly impact its
development trajectory. Sustainable development in Bahrain
is intrinsically linked to broader regional dynamics, including
economic integration, political stability, and environmental
challenges. Regional economic integration supports Bahrain’s
diversification efforts, providing access to larger markets
and investment opportunities, although economic shocks
in neighbouring countries and oil price fluctuations pose
significant risks. Political instability in the region will call for
robust national and regional responses to ensure continued
security and social cohesion. Additionally, environmental
issues such as water scarcity, desertification, dust storms, and
air and marine pollution necessitate regional cooperation, as
Bahrain faces significant risks from climate change, including
rising temperatures and sea levels.

(SDGs 1-5)
Bahrain has exhibited a steadfast commitment to social
development and well-being, positioning these priorities
at the core of its national strategies and action plans. This
commitment is underscored by the allocation of a significant
share of its budget to social sectors, with public social protection
spending equivalent to 5 percent of GDP in 20237. This
expenditure is notably higher compared to regional peers and
underscores Bahrain’s commitment to fostering a supportive
social infrastructure, despite the challenges posed by a high
expatriate population which accounts for more than half of the
total demographic.
Within this context, Bahrain’s commitment to human
development is reflected in its position as a very high human
development country as ranked by the Human Development
Index (HDI), at 34 out of 193 countries and territories. This is
a result of sustained progress over three decades. Between
1990 and 2022, Bahrain’s life expectancy at birth improved
by 6.6 years, expected years of schooling by 3.0 years and
mean years of schooling by 5.9 years between. Gender
disaggregated HDI for Bahrain in 2022 highlights a difference
between males (0.904) and females (0.847) that is driven
largely by the estimated Gross National Income (GNI) per
capita, that for a woman (USD 22,722) was less than a third of
that for a man (USD 64,700).
Bahrain’s educational system boasts near-universal enrolment
rates with opportunities to improve further the quality of
education and alignment with labour market demands.
Initiatives to expand preschool education and the focus on
closing the gender disparity in effective schooling8 are positive
steps towards addressing these gaps.
Healthcare in Bahrain has seen significant advancements, with
life expectancy at birth increasing by more than five years since
2000. The nation has successfully managed communicable
diseases and made strides in addressing noncommunicable
diseases (NCDs), which constitute the leading cause of
death. The Government’s proactive measures to combat the
COVID-19 pandemic and ongoing efforts to tackle NCDs
through public health campaigns against unhealthy diets
and physical inactivity exemplify Bahrain’s commitment to
public health. Moreover, Bahrain’s initiatives to establish a
One-Health team to address antimicrobial resistance, and to
reduce out-of-pocket healthcare expenditures9 indicate the
recognized need for a comprehensive approach to healthcare
sustainability. Recent discussions between the World Health
Organization (WHO) and Bahrain’s Ministry of Health (MoH)
Bahrain highlighted the importance of reinforcing data for
evidence-based public health policy, and strengthening health
diplomacy, collaboration, partnerships, advocacy, and strategic
communications to further enhance Bahrain’s health system.
Heavy reliance on food imports poses a challenge to food
security in Bahrain, primarily due to global volatility of food
prices and vulnerability of global supply chain to disruptions.
The country’s approach to mitigating the impact of rising food
costs and reducing food waste highlights its responsiveness to
transparency remains a critical area for ongoing development.
In the area of environmental protection, addressing the triple
planetary crisis of climate change, biodiversity loss, and
pollution requires more integrated and powerful action plans.
Sustainable management of natural resources and ecosystems
continues to be an area needing further development to ensure
long-term environmental resilience.
Progress in harnessing digitalization, artificial intelligence and
financial inclusion presents opportunities for the country to
accelerate progress across multiple SDGs. A large, educated
youth population also presents a potential to reap the
demographic dividend.

emerging challenges. The social protection system in Bahrain
predominantly benefits nationals, with efforts underway to
progressively extend provisions to expatriate workers. For
example, although migrant workers are excluded from the
pension system, to protect them from abuses in the distribution
of end-of-service (indemnity) benefits the General Authority
for the Social Insurance Organization (SIO) began collecting
end-of-service contributions from employers in March 2024,
with migrant workers then being insured in the private sector.
Furthermore, the SIO itself now disburses end-of-service
benefits to migrant workers, which reduces the vulnerability
of workers to unscrupulous employers. The disparities in
access to social services and housing affordability, particularly
among expatriates and low-income households, underscore
the necessity of a more inclusive social protection framework.
Given the universality of child protection concerns across
the world, the institutional mechanisms for child protection
in Bahrain can be strengthened in compliance with the UN
Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Urban planning and housing policies are evolving to address
the challenges of high population density and environmental
sustainability. The development of public transportation and
public spaces, alongside initiatives to ensure affordable
housing, reflect Bahrain’s strategic approach to urban
development and social inclusion.
Bahrain’s rapid population growth, alongside its high density
and demographic, creates a unique social dynamic calling for
tailored social inclusion strategies. Over half of the population
are expatriates (52 percent), the vast majority of them male
(71 percent)
10
, creating a complex demographic structure.
This diversity, combined with the country’s spatially uneven
population distribution and the specific challenges faced by
non-Bahraini residents, highlight the criticality of addressing
vulnerabilities to achieve the pledge of LNOB. According to the
international human rights treaty body observations, key drivers
for exclusion in any country may include specific national laws
and practices which have a disproportionately negative impact
on disadvantaged groups; prevailing social norms, beliefs
and discriminatory attitudes; limited capacity of duty-bearers
to deliver policies aimed at inclusion; limited participation of
rights-holders in decision making; capacity of service providers
to deliver public services, especially to the most vulnerable
people11; and lack of arrangements for ensuring cooperation
between policymakers and civil society organizations. Some
of these issues will need to be addressed in Bahrain as well.
Consequently, Bahrain has adopted measures aimed at
harmonizing its policies with global standards and responding
proactively to the diverse needs of its population. These efforts
are pivotal for Bahrain to fulfil the 2030 Agenda objectives and
to ensure that no one is left behind.
Addressing the existing educational, protection systems

Bahrain’s governance and political landscape is marked
by both strengths and challenges as it seeks to fulfil its
commitments to security, stability, and human rights within a
complex regional and international framework. The country has
established strong institutional frameworks and has engaged in
efforts to promote human rights, as evidenced by the creation
of the National Institution for Human Rights (NIHR) and the
development of the NHRAP, positioning Bahrain as a regional
leader in these areas. Areas for further progress include
strengthening of institutional mechanisms and processes
including improving the compliance of NIHR with the Paris
Principles. Other areas for further progress to achieve SDG 16
include voice, accountability, and addressing corruption.
The judiciary and law enforcement sectors have seen reforms
aimed at improving justice delivery. Particularly progressive are
the measures around the introduction of alternative penalties
and restorative justice for children. New initiatives on socioeconomic reintegration of prisoners subject to a royal pardon,

Ombudsman in the Ministry of Interior indicate further progress.
Bahrain’s efforts towards human rights advancement and
governance reforms are commendable, yet significant strides
are needed to enhance political participation, transparency,
and accountability. Addressing the challenges will be essential
for Bahrain to achieve a more inclusive, stable, and democratic
society, aligned with SDG 16 and broader international human
rights standards.
Opportunities for Achieving the 2030 Agenda
Bahrain has demonstrated strong political commitment
towards achieving sustainable development by 2030 and
made progress in the various sustainable development
dimensions. The country boasts a well-educated population
with greater potential, particularly among women and young
people. Further prioritization in human capital is crucial for
building a resilient and skilled workforce, including enhanced
investment in health services, education, and support for
people with vulnerabilities17. Social protection programs require
optimization to promote solidarity and buffer economic shocks
for people with vulnerabilities18, including low-skilled expatriate
workers.
Bahrain unveiled an ambitious energy transition agenda
that encompasses three broad principles: improving energy
efficiency, increasing renewables’ share and deploying
technologies to reduce emissions, and launched the voluntary
carbon offsetting platform. Given the country’s reliance on
desalination and groundwater abstraction for water supplies, it
is crucial to focus on energy consumption for water desalination
and policies to manage the water-energy nexus more
sustainably. Investments in green development and effective
natural resource management are essential to mitigate
the impacts of climate change and ensure environmental
sustainability.
Bahrain’s economic diversification efforts have seen successful,
particularly in the financial sector and fintech ecosystem.
Further reforms in labour markets, education, and immigration
policies are needed to boost productivity and economic
opportunities for Bahrainis. Improving the fiscal balance and
implementing climate-friendly diversification efforts are crucial
for achieving long-term financial stability and improving living
standards.
Bahrain has been engaging with the United Nations human
rights institutions and treaty bodies and has adopted its first
NHRAP. It is important to support these efforts by ensuring the
availability of strong implementation capacity and monitoring
mechanisms. The Government’s focus on security measures
and social benefits helps ensure social stability in the country.
Improving governance, enhancing human rights, and ensuring
greater political participation are vital for addressing societal
grievances and promoting peace and stability.
In conclusion, Bahrain’s journey towards achieving Agenda
2030 requires a balanced approach across all dimensions of
sustainable development. By leveraging its human capital,
addressing environmental challenges, diversifying its economy,
promoting peace and governance, and strengthening
partnerships, Bahrain can overcome structural challenges and
ensure no one is left behind in its development progress.

ANNEX D: Summary
of Consultations
Introduction
In preparation for the Bahrain UNSDCF 2025-2029,
the United Nations in Bahrain undertook extensive
consultations with around 100 people (including 40
women) among youth, civil society representatives,
workers and employers’ unions, and the private sector.
The consultations revealed a robust collective desire for
a United Nations presence that is not only responsive but
also proactively inclusive and strategically aligned with
Bahrain’s national priorities. Notably, the consultations
employed innovative approaches to ensure active
participation from youth groups, workers, unions, and
populations with higher needs71, thus reflecting a broad
and diverse range of voices in the framework.
People – Enhanced Social Equity and Well-Being:
Feedback from the consultations indicated a critical need
for comprehensive data management to address social
equity challenges effectively. Stakeholders expressed a
desire for the United Nations to support capacity-building
initiatives that empower local solutions and improve
service delivery in health (including mental health),
education, and social protection, ensuring that benefits
reach all segments of the population.
Prosperity – Sustainable Economic Transformation:
Stakeholders underscored the importance of nurturing
entrepreneurshipanddigital skills tomeetevolvingmarket
demands. There was a strong call for the United Nations
to facilitate knowledge exchange and capacity building,
especially in digital transformation and sustainable
business practices. Participants also stressed the need
for educational reforms to align more closely with labour
market requirements, thereby enhancing economic
opportunities for all, particularly populations with higher
needs72.
Peace – Governance for Justice and Human Rights:
Participants advocated for stronger policies to protect
the rights of expatriate workers and people with
disabilities, emphasizing the need for wage protection
laws and improved infrastructural accessibility. Feedback
highlighted the importance of the United Nations’ role
in fostering policy reforms, raising awareness of rights
among people with vulnerabilities73, and ensuring
inclusivity in governance processes.
Planet – Resilient Environmental Stewardship: Discussion
in this area focused on the urgent need for sustainable
environmental practices. Participants recommended that
theUnitedNations supportefforts to implementguidelines
for sustainable construction, promote circular economy
initiatives, and enhance education on environmental
conservation. There was a strong advocacy for the
United Nations to lead by example in facilitating crosssector collaboration to protect and sustainably manage
Bahrain’s natural resources.
Leave No One Behind: The consultations highlighted
the importance of including the perspectives of
people with vulnerabilities74 to ensure that no one is
left behind. Participants noted the role of women and
youth as change agents, discussing specific needs and
challenges faced by these groups. The issues of the
transition of young people into the job market came up
repeatedly. Different groups highlighted the needs of
individuals on the neurodivergent spectrum, with calls
for policies and programs to provide tailored support and
enhance their access to educational and employment
opportunities. Additionally, stakeholders emphasized
the need to address gender disparities, by specific focus
on empowering women through entrepreneurship and
leadership programmes, and ensuring equitable access
to social services for women and girls. The unique
challenges faced by expatriate workers, low-income
households, and families with children with disabilities
were highlighted, advocating for enhanced social
protection measures and accessible public services.
These detailed discussions have been integral in
shaping the strategic priorities of the UNSDCF, ensuring
that the framework is responsive to the diverse needs of
Bahrain’s population.
